issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette: At 80 years old, Leilani still wakes up in the dead of night, her heart racing, as she lies in bed and listens for the sound of footsteps outside her bedroom door. It's a habit she's developed over the decades since her ex-husband, a man she thought she loved, would sneak into their bedroom and attack her while she slept. Leilani had been a welder, with hands that could shape metal and fix broken things, but after years of abuse, she began to feel like her own body was the broken thing. She remembers one night in particular when he'd come home drunk and angry, his eyes blazing as he towered over her in bed. She'd tried to defend herself, but he was too strong, and the memory of his grip on her wrists still makes her skin crawl. Leilani had thought she'd left all that behind when she finally found the courage to leave him, but the memories lingered, etched into her mind like scars. Years later, even in her own home with her new husband, a kind and gentle man who loves her dearly, Leilani can't shake off the feeling of being on guard. She'll be watching TV or cooking dinner when suddenly she's back in that bedroom, waiting for the sound of footsteps, waiting for the pain to begin again. Her mind tells her it's irrational, that she's safe now, but her body doesn't seem to agree. She's come to believe that her body has been permanently damaged by what happened, that some essential part of her was broken and can never be fixed. It's a feeling that makes her avoid intimacy with her husband, fearing that he'll somehow see the damage, that he'll know she's not whole anymore. She's lost touch with her own emotions, too, as if they've been locked away in a box she can't quite reach. Sometimes, Leilani will be out running errands or visiting friends when suddenly she's hit with a wave of anxiety, her heart racing and her palms sweating. It's as if her body has decided to betray her again, reminding her that it can't be trusted. She'll quickly make an excuse and head home, feeling like she needs to retreat to the safety of her own space. Her husband has been patient with her, trying to understand what she's going through, but Leilani knows he doesn't get it. How could he? He wasn't there in that bedroom, fighting for his life. Sometimes she feels like she's living two separate lives: one as a happy wife and friend, the other as a survivor of something terrible. Leilani's trouble sleeping has become so chronic that her doctor has prescribed her medication, but even with the pills, she finds herself waking up multiple times a night to check whether she's safe. It's exhausting, but what frightens her most is the thought of losing control again, of being trapped in that nightmare world where she's at the mercy of someone else. It was after a particularly bad episode, when Leilani found herself shaking and crying uncontrollably, that she realized she needed help. She couldn't keep living like this, trapped by memories and fears that seemed to have no end. With her husband's support, she finally reached out for therapy, hoping to find a way to quiet the voices in her head, to learn how to trust herself again.
